subject: physics_2
question_text: State the working principle of potentiometer explain with the help of circuit diagram. How the emf of two primary cells are compared by using the potentiometer.

verification.note: The 2+2+2+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Transcription (book p29, LAQ 2): the wording is kept as printed, including 'How the emf of two primary cells are compared'; the book's 'manganine', 'Comparision' and 'inseries' spellings are corrected on the card. NOTE ON ρ: the book uses ρ for the RESISTANCE PER UNIT LENGTH of the potentiometer wire (ρ = R/L), not for resistivity; the card says so in words wherever ρ appears. Hand-checked: ε₁ = Iρl₁ and ε₂ = Iρl₂ with the same primary current, so ε₁/ε₂ = l₁/l₂.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The principle
steps.mark_note: V ∝ l for a steady current
lines: Principle: when a steady current passes
through a wire of uniform cross section, the
potential difference between any two points
on the wire is directly proportional to the
length of wire between those points.
The constant of proportionality is called the
potential gradient of the wire.
steps.margin_note: First two marks. State the principle in full: steady current, uniform cross section, V ∝ l.
steps.why: A uniform wire has the same resistance in every centimetre, so a steady current produces the same potential drop in every centimetre. Adding equal drops over l centimetres makes the total drop proportional to l.
common_mistakes: Leaving out uniform cross section. Without it the drop per centimetre is not the same everywhere.

recall.must_convey: That with a steady current in a wire of uniform cross section the potential difference between two points is proportional to the length between them.
accept: potential difference is proportional to length
reject: epsilon one by epsilon two equals l one by l two

steps.memory_tip: Same wire, same current: every centimetre drops the same voltage.

steps.label: The primary circuit
steps.margin_note: The thick line is the potentiometer wire AB. The cell E, the key and the rheostat Rₕ send a steady current I through it.
steps.why: The primary circuit does one job: it holds a steady, adjustable current in the wire so that the potential gradient stays fixed while the two cells are balanced one after the other.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the rheostat, which is what makes the gradient adjustable.

recall.must_convey: That the primary circuit is the wire AB with a cell, a key and a rheostat across its ends.
accept: draw the wire A B with the cell and rheostat
primary circuit across the ends of the wire

steps.memory_tip: Primary circuit first: it sets the gradient before anything is measured.

steps.label: The secondary circuit
steps.margin_note: Both cells are joined by their positive ends to A. Each branch carries its own key, and the jockey slides along AB.
steps.why: Both cells face the wire the same way round, so each of them opposes the drop along AB and can be brought to a balance point of its own.
common_mistakes: Joining the two cells with opposite ends to A, so no balance point can be found.

recall.must_convey: That the secondary circuit has the two cells with their keys joined through a galvanometer to the jockey on AB.
accept: two cells with keys and a galvanometer
secondary circuit from A through the cells to the jockey
reject: cell and rheostat across A B

steps.memory_tip: Same ends to A, one key closed at a time.

steps.label: The arrangement
lines: A uniform manganin wire AB about 10 m long is
fixed on a wooden plank beside a metre scale.
Its ends carry copper strips of negligible
resistance.
The ends A and B are joined to a cell of emf E
and internal resistance r through a key K and
a rheostat. This is the primary circuit.
With Rₛ the series resistance and R the
resistance of the whole wire of length L,
Writing ρ = R/L for the resistance per unit
length, the drop across a length l is
so the potential gradient of the wire is
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The wire and its primary circuit, then the potential gradient V/l = Iρ.
steps.why: The gradient depends only on the primary circuit, so as long as the rheostat is left alone it is the same for both cells. That is what allows the two balancing lengths to be compared directly.
common_mistakes: Using ρ for resistivity. Here ρ means resistance per unit length, R/L.
Changing the rheostat setting between the two readings.

recall.must_convey: That a uniform wire AB carries a steady current from the primary circuit and its potential gradient is I times the resistance per unit length.
accept: uniform wire about ten metre on a plank
current is E by r plus R plus R s
reject: epsilon one equals I rho l one

steps.memory_tip: Gradient = current × resistance per centimetre. Fix it once and leave it alone.

steps.label: The two balance points
lines: The secondary circuit holds the two cells ε₁
and ε₂ with the plug keys K₁ and K₂, joined
through a galvanometer G to the jockey J.
Close K and K₁ only. Slide the jockey along
AB until the galvanometer reads zero. Let the
balancing length from A be l₁. Then
Now open K₁ and close K₂, without touching
the rheostat. The new balancing length is l₂,
so
steps.margin_note: Two marks. One key at a time, zero deflection each time, and one equation per reading.
steps.why: At the balance point the drop along the length l exactly opposes the cell, so no current passes through the galvanometer and the cell's own internal resistance carries no current. This is why the reading is the emf and not the terminal voltage.
common_mistakes: Closing both keys together. The two cells must be balanced one at a time.
Calling the balanced value the terminal voltage. At zero galvanometer current it is the emf.

recall.must_convey: That each cell in turn is balanced at zero deflection, giving epsilon one equals I rho l one and epsilon two equals I rho l two.
accept: close K one get balance at l one
epsilon one equals I rho l one
epsilon two equals I rho l two
reject: epsilon one by epsilon two equals l one by l two

steps.memory_tip: One key, one balance, one equation. Then repeat for the other cell.

steps.label: The result
lines: Dividing (1) by (2), the current I and the
resistance per unit length ρ cancel:

lines.text: ε₁/ε₂ = I ρ l₁ / I ρ l₂

lines: So the emfs of the two cells are compared by
measuring the two balancing lengths on the
metre scale. If one emf is known, the other
follows from this ratio.
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Show I and ρ cancelling, then box the ratio.
steps.why: Neither the primary current nor the resistance of the wire needs to be measured, because both cancel in the division. The whole measurement is reduced to two lengths read off a metre scale, which is why the method is so accurate.
common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio. The longer balancing length belongs to the larger emf.
Stopping at the two separate equations without dividing them.

recall.must_convey: That dividing the two equations cancels I and rho and leaves epsilon one by epsilon two equal to l one by l two.
accept: epsilon one by epsilon two equals l one by l two
ratio of emfs equals ratio of lengths
reject: epsilon one equals I rho l one

steps.memory_tip: Divide the two readings and everything but the lengths cancels.

insider_note: The two marks in the last step are for showing I and ρ cancelling. An answer that stops at the two separate balance equations has not compared anything.
